label: Steps a day
body:
Heart and longevity benefits climb
steeply up to about 8,000 steps.
No gym needed. A 10-min walk after
meals also blunts sugar spikes.
caption:
You don't need 10,000 steps. But you probably need more than you're doing.

The 10k number came from a 1960s pedometer ad — not science.

What large studies actually show: the risk of early death drops steeply as daily steps rise, and the benefit starts levelling off around 7,000–8,000 steps for most adults.

Easy ways to get there:
→ 10-minute walk after each meal
→ Take calls standing or walking
→ Stairs instead of the lift
→ Park or get off one stop early

Walking is the most underrated health habit there is.

Vitamin D

India gets more sunshine than most countries. So why are most Indians low on vitamin D?

→ 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, a few times a week

Fruit juice is
healthy?

That "100% natural" juice box isn't the health drink it looks like.

Juicing strips out the fibre — the part that slows sugar down.

What happens without the fibre:
→ Sugar hits your blood fast
→ You're hungry again soon
→ It's easy to drink 3 oranges' worth in 30 seconds

Sleeping badly even though you're exhausted? Check when you had your last chai.

→ Reduces deep sleep
→ Makes sleep lighter and more broken
→ Leaves you groggy the next morning
→ So you reach for more caffeine… and repeat

Veg diet covers

Vitamin B12.

→ Stronger bones and joints
→ Better blood sugar control
→ Higher resting metabolism

label: Did you know
headline:
Rest days
build muscle.

Training hard every single day and not seeing results? You might need less, not more.

Skip recovery and you get:
→ Stalled strength
→ Constant soreness
→ Poor sleep and low energy
→ Higher injury risk

The rule of thumb: about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Walking and stretching on rest days is great.

→ 10 minutes of morning sunlight

label: Did you know
headline:
Your resting
heart rate talks.
body: Normal is 60–100 bpm, and fitter people sit lower. If yours stays higher than usual for days, it can signal poor sleep, stress or illness.
caption:
Your resting heart rate is one of the simplest health signals you can track — and it's free.

Measure it in the morning, before getting out of bed.

What the numbers mean:
→ 60–100 bpm is the normal adult range
→ Regular exercise usually brings it lower over time
→ A rise of several beats for days can mean poor sleep, stress, dehydration or an oncoming illness

Track it for a week to learn your baseline. Changes matter more than one reading.

label: Healthy blood pressure
body:
Below 120/80 mmHg is ideal.
140/90 or above on repeat checks
is high BP. It rarely has symptoms,
so the only way to know is to check.
caption:
High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. Most people with it feel completely fine.

Until a heart attack or stroke.

What the numbers mean:
→ Below 120/80 — ideal
→ 120–139 / 80–89 — higher than ideal, time to act
→ 140/90 or above on repeat readings — high blood pressure

What brings it down:
→ Less salt (pickles, papad, namkeen, packaged food)
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Losing even a few kg if you're overweight
→ Less alcohol, no smoking

Every adult should know their number. Get it checked at least once a year.

label: Wellbeing
headline:
Breathe out
the stress
body: Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6. A longer exhale slows your heart rate and calms you down. Five minutes is enough.
caption:
Feeling wound up before a meeting, an exam or a tough conversation? Your breath is the fastest off-switch you have.

And it's free.

When you breathe out slowly, your heart rate drops a little and your body shifts out of "fight or flight".

Try it right now:
→ Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts
→ Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 counts
→ Keep your shoulders relaxed
→ Repeat for 5 minutes

Eating late
makes you fat?

"Don't eat after 7 PM or you'll gain weight." Heard this one?

Your body doesn't have a clock that turns food into fat after sunset.

Weight change comes from your total calories over days and weeks — not the time on the clock.

Why late eating gets the blame:
→ Late-night snacking is usually extra food, not a meal
→ It's often chips, sweets and biscuits
→ A heavy dinner right before bed can cause acidity and poor sleep
→ Poor sleep makes you hungrier the next day

The smart move: eat dinner 2–3 hours before bed and keep it balanced. If you're truly hungry later, curd, fruit or a handful of nuts.

How many teaspoons of sugar do you have a day? Most people have no idea.

→ Chai and coffee (2 tsp a cup adds up fast)
→ Biscuits, rusks and "healthy" cereals

→ Ketchup, sauces and flavoured yoghurt

→ Reduce sugar in chai by half a spoon every week
→ Swap biscuits for fruit or nuts
→ Water or chaas instead of cold drinks

label: Reality check
headline:
Multigrain means
healthy?
body: Many multigrain breads and biscuits are mostly maida with a sprinkle of other grains. Check the ingredients list — the first item is the main one.
caption:
"Multigrain" on the pack sounds healthy. But it doesn't mean whole grain.

It just means more than one grain is in there — even if it's a tiny amount.

Many multigrain breads, biscuits and atta blends are mostly refined flour (maida) with a little oats, ragi or flax added for the label.

How to check in 10 seconds:
→ Read the ingredients list — they're listed from most to least
→ First ingredient should be "whole wheat" or another whole grain
→ "Wheat flour" or "refined wheat flour" usually means maida
→ Compare fibre: aim for 6 g or more per 100 g

Trust the ingredients, not the front of the pack.

→ Full push-ups

Move to the next level when you can do 3 clean sets of 10.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your ears clean
themselves.
body: Ear wax moves out on its own as you chew and talk. Cotton buds push it deeper and can hurt your eardrum. Just wipe the outer ear.
caption:
Cleaning your ears with cotton buds every day? You're probably doing more harm than good.

Ear wax isn't dirt. It traps dust, keeps the ear canal moist and helps fight infection.

Your ears are self-cleaning: jaw movement slowly pushes old wax outwards.

What cotton buds actually do:
→ Push wax deeper, causing blockages
→ Scratch the delicate skin of the ear canal
→ Can damage your eardrum

What to do instead:
→ Wipe the outer ear with a cloth after a bath
→ Never put hairpins, keys or oil drops inside
→ See a doctor for pain, blocked hearing or discharge

Leave your ears alone. They've got this.

label: HbA1c warning line
body:
HbA1c shows your average sugar
over the last 2–3 months.
Below 5.7% normal. 5.7–6.4%
prediabetes. 6.5%+ diabetes.
caption:
A fasting sugar test shows one morning. HbA1c shows the last 2–3 months.

That's why doctors trust it.

HbA1c measures how much sugar has stuck to your red blood cells, which live about 3 months.

What the result means:
→ Below 5.7% — normal
→ 5.7% to 6.4% — prediabetes
→ 6.5% or higher — diabetes (confirmed by your doctor)

Prediabetes is the window where lifestyle changes work best:
→ Lose 5–7% of your body weight if overweight
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Fewer refined carbs and sugary drinks

Over 30, or diabetes in the family? Ask for an HbA1c test.

headline:
Heart attack
warning signs

sections.title: Chest
sections.text: Pressure, squeezing or pain lasting minutes.

sections.title: Spreading
sections.text: To the arm, jaw, neck or back.

sections.title: With
sections.text: Breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea.

caption:
Knowing these signs can save a life — maybe someone at home.

In a heart attack, every minute matters.

Common warning signs:
→ Chest pressure, squeezing or pain that lasts more than a few minutes
→ Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back or upper stomach
→ Shortness of breath
→ Cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness

Women, older people and people with diabetes often have milder or unusual symptoms — like only breathlessness, tiredness or "gas".

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112 straight away
→ Don't drive yourself to hospital
→ Don't wait to "see if it passes"

Carbs make

caption:
Rice, roti and fruit aren't the enemy. Cutting all carbs isn't the secret to fat loss.

Weight gain comes from eating more calories than you use — whether they come from carbs, fat or protein.

→ Huge portions of white rice or maida
→ Sugary drinks, sweets and biscuits
→ Fried snacks (carbs + oil = easy to overeat)
→ Carbs with almost no protein or vegetables

→ Dal, rajma, chana
→ Fruit and vegetables
→ Millets, oats, whole wheat roti

The fix isn't zero carbs. It's better carbs, sensible portions, and protein on the plate.

caption:
Your waist size may say more about your health than your weight does.

That fat is linked to diabetes, heart disease and fatty liver.

→ Stand straight and breathe out normally

→ Tape snug, not pressing into the skin

Curd for

Curd (dahi).

Tea with meals
blocks iron.
body: Tannins in tea and coffee cut how much iron you absorb from food. Keep a one-hour gap. Pair dal or greens with lemon or amla instead.
caption:
Chai right after lunch is a habit for many of us. It may be costing you iron.

Tea and coffee contain tannins and polyphenols. They bind to the iron in plant foods and reduce how much your body absorbs.

This matters a lot in India, where anaemia is very common — especially in women.

→ Keep a gap of about an hour between meals and chai or coffee
→ Add vitamin C to iron-rich meals: lemon, amla, guava, tomato
→ Eat iron-rich foods: dal, chana, rajma, green leafy veg, ragi

label: Safe level of alcohol

for health. Risk of cancer and
other harm starts from the first
drink and rises with every one.

"A drink a day is good for the heart." That idea hasn't held up.

Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen — the same category as tobacco.

→ At least 7 types of cancer, including breast and bowel
→ High blood pressure and heart rhythm problems
→ Fatty liver and liver disease
→ Poor sleep, weight gain and low mood

If you drink:
→ Less is always better
→ Have alcohol-free days every week
→ Never drink and drive

label: Sleep
headline:
Can't sleep?
Get up.
body: Lying awake teaches your brain that bed means stress. Get up, sit somewhere dim and calm, and go back only when you're sleepy.
caption:
Tossing and turning for an hour? Staying in bed is making it worse.

When you lie awake night after night, your brain starts linking your bed with frustration, not sleep.

Sleep doctors use a simple rule:
→ If you're awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed
→ Sit somewhere dim and quiet
→ Read a paper book or listen to something calm — no phone
→ Go back to bed only when you feel sleepy
→ Repeat if needed

Also: keep the same wake-up time, even after a bad night.

Sweating more

body: Sweat is how your body cools down, not how it burns fat. The weight you lose is water, and it comes back as soon as you drink.
caption:
Wearing a sweat suit or working out in a hot room to "melt the fat"? It doesn't work like that.

Sweat is water your body releases to cool down.

How much you sweat depends on heat, humidity, genetics and fitness — not on how much fat you're burning.

What really happens:
→ You lose water weight
→ The scale drops for a few hours
→ You drink water, and it comes right back
→ Too much sweating can leave you dehydrated and dizzy

What does burn fat: a consistent calorie deficit, strength training, daily movement and enough protein.

label: BMI cutoff for Indians
body:
For Asian Indians, BMI 23–24.9
counts as overweight, 25+ as obese.
The global cutoffs (25/30) miss
risk that starts earlier for us.
caption:
Your BMI says "normal"? For Indians, the usual chart can be misleading.

Asian Indians tend to develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations.

That's why Indian guidelines use lower cutoffs:
→ 18.5–22.9 — normal
→ 23–24.9 — overweight
→ 25 and above — obese

How to calculate: weight (kg) ÷ height (m) ÷ height (m).

label: Reality check
headline:
Protein bars are
health food?
body: Many protein bars carry as much sugar and calories as a chocolate bar. Check the label. A handful of nuts, chana or curd often does better.
caption:
That protein bar in your gym bag might be a chocolate bar in disguise.

Many popular bars contain:
→ 10–20 g of sugar or syrups
→ 200–300 calories
→ Less protein than the front of the pack suggests
→ Sugar alcohols that can cause bloating

Your bones
are alive.

Bones aren't dead scaffolding. They're living tissue that rebuilds itself every day.

Your body is always breaking down old bone and laying down new bone.

→ Strength training and impact (walking, stairs, skipping)

→ Vitamin D from sunlight (and testing if you're low)

caption:
Tuition, homework, screens — where's the time to play? Children need it more than ever.

WHO recommends that children and teens aged 5–17 get at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day.

What counts:
→ Running, cycling, skipping
→ Football, cricket, badminton, kabaddi
→ Dancing, swimming
→ Brisk walking to school

At least 3 days a week should include activities that strengthen muscles and bones, like jumping and climbing.

Why it matters:
→ Better focus and grades
→ Stronger bones and heart
→ Better sleep and mood
→ Lower risk of childhood obesity

Play is not a waste of time.

Running ruins

"Don't run, you'll ruin your knees." It's one of the most common warnings — and the evidence doesn't back it up.

→ Doing too much too soon
→ Weak hips and thighs
→ Running through sharp pain
→ Carrying a lot of extra weight

label: Fever starts here
body:
A temperature of 38°C (100.4°F)
or higher counts as a fever.
Rest and fluids help. See a doctor
if it lasts 3 days or is very high.
caption:
Feeling warm? A thermometer settles it. Not every warm forehead is a fever.

Normal body temperature is around 37°C (98.6°F), and it changes a little through the day.

A fever is usually 38°C (100.4°F) or higher.

What helps at home:
→ Rest
→ Plenty of fluids — water, ORS, soups, coconut water
→ Light clothing and a cool room

See a doctor if:
→ Fever lasts more than 3 days
→ It's 39.4°C (103°F) or higher
→ There's a rash, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or trouble breathing
→ It's an infant, older person, or someone with a long-term illness

During dengue season, don't ignore a fever.

Weekend lie-ins
fix sleep debt?

Five short nights, then sleeping till noon on Sunday? That's not catching up — it's jet lag at home.

Extra sleep at the weekend can ease some tiredness. But it doesn't fully undo a week of short sleep.

And a big shift in your wake time confuses your body clock. Scientists call it "social jet lag".

→ Hard to fall asleep on Sunday night
→ Groggy Monday mornings
→ More cravings and lower mood

A better plan:
→ Keep weekend wake time within an hour of weekdays
→ Take a short afternoon nap if you need it
→ Fix weekday sleep, rather than repaying it later

Consistency beats catch-up.

Beat
constipation

→ Sitting all day
→ Ignoring the urge to go

After an 8-hour fast:
Under 100 mg/dL is normal.

126 or more on 2 tests: diabetes.

A fasting blood sugar test is cheap, quick and tells you a lot.

→ Below 100 mg/dL — normal
→ 100 to 125 mg/dL — prediabetes

→ Daily walking and strength training
→ Less sugar and refined carbs
→ More protein, fibre and vegetables
→ Losing weight if you carry extra around the waist

A good warm-up takes just 5–10 minutes and makes your workout safer and better.

→ Raises your body temperature and heart rate
→ Gets your joints moving freely
→ Wakes up the muscles you're about to use

→ 3–5 minutes of brisk walking, light jogging or skipping
→ Arm circles, leg swings, hip circles, bodyweight squats
→ 1–2 lighter sets of your first exercise

label: Myth buster
headline:
No pain,
no gain?
body: Effort should feel hard, but pain is a warning. Sharp, sudden or joint pain means stop. Progress comes from steady effort over months.
caption:
"No pain, no gain" sounds tough. It also causes a lot of injuries.

There's a big difference between effort and pain.

Normal (keep going):
→ Muscles burning near the end of a set
→ Heavy breathing during cardio
→ Mild soreness 1–2 days later

Warning signs (stop):
→ Sharp or stabbing pain
→ Pain in a joint, not a muscle
→ Pain that gets worse as you continue
→ Swelling, or pain that lasts more than a few days

Results come from training consistently for months — not from destroying yourself in one session.

label: Days to a habit

Not 21. In one study, new habits
took 66 days on average to stick —
from 18 to 254 days. Missing
a day now and then is fine.
caption:
"It takes 21 days to build a habit." That number has no real science behind it.

A University College London study followed people building new daily habits, like drinking water with lunch or going for a run.

On average, it took 66 days for a habit to become automatic. Some took 18 days, others more than 250.

The good news:
→ Missing a single day didn't derail the habit
→ Simple habits stuck faster than complex ones

How to make habits stick:
→ Start tiny (2 push-ups, not 50)
→ Tie it to something you already do ("after brushing, I…")
→ Same time, same place
→ Track it on a calendar

Give it two months, not three weeks.

Herbal means

"It's herbal, so it can't harm." Many people think this. It isn't always true.

Plants contain active compounds — that's why some work. It's also why they can cause problems.

→ Interactions with blood thinners, diabetes or BP medicines
→ Liver damage with some concentrated extracts
→ Contamination or wrong doses in poorly made products
→ Stopping prescribed medicine because a supplement "will do"

Stay safe:
→ Buy from trusted, licensed brands
→ Tell your doctor about every supplement, powder or kadha you take regularly
→ Never stop prescribed medicine without advice
→ Be wary of anything promising a "cure"

Your gut and
brain talk.

Ever had butterflies before a big moment, or needed the toilet before an exam? That's your gut-brain connection.

→ Gut problems can affect your mood and energy
→ IBS symptoms often get worse with stress

WHO: breast milk alone for the
first 6 months — no water, honey
or ghutti. Then add solid foods
and continue to 2 years or beyond.

For a baby's first six months, breast milk is all they need. Not even water.

WHO and UNICEF recommend:
→ Starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth
→ Only breast milk for the first 6 months
→ Adding safe, nutritious solid foods from 6 months
→ Continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond

→ Water, even in summer (breast milk is mostly water)
→ Honey, ghutti or janam ghutti
→ Animal milk or other drinks

Breastfeeding protects babies against infections and benefits mothers too.

label: Women's health

PCOS: the
basics
body: Irregular periods, acne, extra hair and weight gain are common signs. Losing even 5–10% of body weight can improve cycles and symptoms.
caption:
PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is one of the most common hormone conditions in women of reproductive age.

Common signs:
→ Irregular or missed periods
→ Acne and oily skin
→ Extra hair on the face or body
→ Weight gain, especially around the belly
→ Thinning hair on the scalp

PCOS is closely linked to insulin resistance, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes later.

What helps most people:
→ Losing 5–10% of body weight, if overweight
→ Strength training and daily walking
→ Protein and fibre in every meal, fewer refined carbs
→ Regular sleep

If you think you have PCOS, see a gynaecologist. Treatment is available.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Cold water after
meals = fat?
body: Cold water does not turn food into fat or "freeze" it in your stomach. Drink water at whatever temperature you like, with or after meals.
caption:
"Never drink cold water after eating — it solidifies the fat." This one gets forwarded a lot.

It isn't true.

Your stomach quickly brings any drink to body temperature. Cold water doesn't make food harder to digest, and it doesn't cause weight gain.

What's true:
→ Water with meals is fine and can help you feel full
→ Warm water may feel more soothing to some people — that's preference
→ Some people with certain throat or oesophagus conditions find cold drinks uncomfortable

What matters more for digestion:
→ Eating slowly
→ Fibre and enough water through the day
→ Not lying down right after a big meal

Drink water. Any temperature.

label: Indians with fatty liver
body:
Studies estimate about 1 in 3
Indian adults has fatty liver,
often with no symptoms — even at
a normal weight. It is reversible.
caption:
Fatty liver is far more common than most people realise — and it usually has no symptoms.

Studies estimate that about 1 in 3 Indian adults has non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, where fat builds up in the liver.

Who's at higher risk:
→ People with a large waist or excess weight
→ People with diabetes or prediabetes
→ High triglycerides
→ Even "thin" people with belly fat

Left unchecked, it can lead to liver inflammation and scarring.

The good news — it's often reversible:
→ Losing 7–10% of body weight can reduce liver fat significantly
→ Daily activity
→ Cut sugary drinks, sweets and refined carbs
→ Avoid alcohol

Ask your doctor about a liver check if you're at risk.

label: Reality check

Thyroid is why
you gain weight?
body: An underactive thyroid can add a few kilos, often fluid. Once treated, it shouldn't block fat loss. Get tested, then focus on habits.
caption:
"I can't lose weight because of my thyroid." Sometimes there's some truth to it — but usually less than people think.

Hypothyroidism (an underactive thyroid) slows metabolism and can cause modest weight gain, partly from fluid.

Once it's diagnosed and treated, thyroid levels return to normal — and weight loss works the same way as for anyone else.

Signs worth testing for:
→ Tiredness and feeling cold
→ Dry skin and hair fall
→ Constipation
→ Irregular periods
→ Unexplained weight gain

What to do:
→ Get a TSH test
→ Take medicine exactly as prescribed
→ Then focus on food, movement and sleep

Your thyroid isn't a life sentence for weight.

label: Did you know
headline:
One-leg balance
predicts health.
body: In a large study of middle-aged and older adults, those who could not stand on one leg for 10 seconds had a higher risk of dying earlier.

Can you stand on one leg for 10 seconds? It's a simple test with a surprising link to health.

A 2022 study followed over 1,700 adults aged 51–75. Those who couldn't balance on one leg for 10 seconds were significantly more likely to die over the next 7 years than those who could.

Balance reflects strength, coordination and overall fitness — and it declines with age if not used.

Try it (near a wall for safety):
→ Stand on one foot, other foot resting behind the standing leg
→ Arms by your sides, eyes forward
→ Aim for 10 seconds on each leg

label: Total cholesterol

Total under 200. LDL under 100.
HDL over 40 (men), 50 (women).

Got a lipid profile report and not sure what it means? Here's a quick guide.

Typical healthy targets (mg/dL):
→ Total cholesterol: below 200
→ LDL ("bad"): below 100 — lower if your doctor advises
→ HDL ("good"): above 40 for men, above 50 for women
→ Triglycerides: below 150

What helps:
→ Cut trans fats (vanaspati, bakery and fried snacks)
→ More fibre — oats, dal, fruit, vegetables
→ Daily activity
→ Less sugar and refined carbs (they push triglycerides up)
→ No smoking

Adults should get tested, and more often if heart disease runs in the family.

Fat-free means

"Fat-free" and "low-fat" on the pack — that must be the healthy choice, right? Not always.

→ Fat-free biscuits with similar calories to regular ones

label: Heatstroke danger

Body temperature of 40°C or more
with confusion or no sweating is
heatstroke — an emergency.
Cool the person and call 108.
caption:
Indian summers are getting hotter. Knowing the signs of heatstroke can save a life.

Heat exhaustion comes first:
→ Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness
→ Headache, nausea, muscle cramps

Heatstroke is a medical emergency:
→ Body temperature 40°C (104°F) or higher
→ Confusion, slurred speech or fainting
→ Hot, dry skin — sweating may stop
→ Fast heartbeat

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112
→ Move the person to shade or a cool room
→ Cool them fast: wet cloths, fan, cool water on skin
→ Give sips of water only if they're fully alert

Prevent it: avoid the sun from 12 to 4 PM, drink water often, and check on elderly neighbours.

Antibiotics for
a cold?

caption:
Cold, cough, sore throat — and a strip of antibiotics from the chemist? Please don't.

Most colds, flu and sore throats are caused by viruses. Antibiotics only work against bacteria.

Taking them when you don't need them:
→ Won't make you better faster
→ Can cause diarrhoea, acidity and allergic reactions
→ Upsets your gut bacteria
→ Helps create antibiotic-resistant bacteria — a serious and growing problem in India

What helps a cold:
→ Rest and fluids
→ Steam and warm salt-water gargles
→ Honey for cough (not for babies under 1)

Take antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them — and finish the course as told.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your liver can
regrow.
body: The liver can regenerate after injury — even from a partial transplant. But long-term damage from alcohol or fatty liver leaves scars.
caption:
Your liver is the only organ that can regrow lost tissue. It's remarkable — but it has limits.

That's why living-donor liver transplants work: both the donor's and the recipient's liver pieces grow back towards full size.

Your liver handles over 500 jobs, including:
→ Filtering toxins and medicines
→ Storing energy
→ Making proteins that help blood clot
→ Processing fat

But repeated damage — from alcohol, fatty liver, or hepatitis — can cause scarring (cirrhosis) that doesn't heal.

Protect it:
→ Limit or avoid alcohol
→ Keep a healthy waist size
→ Get vaccinated for hepatitis B
→ Don't overuse painkillers or unknown supplements

Phones are the easiest way to keep a toddler quiet. But young brains need something else.

→ Under 2 years: no screen time (video calls with family are fine)
→ 2 to 4 years: no more than 1 hour a day — less is better

→ Active play, several times a day
→ Talking, singing and reading with adults

→ No screens during meals

Spot a
stroke FAST

sections.text: Drooping on one side when smiling.

sections.title: Arms
sections.text: One arm weak or drifting down.

sections.title: Speech

In a stroke, brain cells die every minute without blood supply. Fast action saves lives and function.

→ A — Arms: can they raise both arms? Does one drift down?
→ S — Speech: is it slurred or strange?
→ T — Time: call 108 or 112 immediately

Other sudden signs:
→ Loss of balance or dizziness
→ Sudden blurred or lost vision
→ Severe headache with no known cause

Note the time symptoms started — doctors need it.

Don't wait for symptoms to pass. Don't give food or water. Get to a hospital with a stroke unit.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Microwaving kills
nutrients?
body: All cooking changes nutrients. Microwaving is quick and uses little water, so it often keeps more vitamins than long boiling. Use safe containers.
caption:
Some people avoid microwaves because they "destroy nutrients". It's actually one of the gentler ways to cook.

Every cooking method affects nutrients. The biggest losses happen with:
→ Long cooking times
→ High heat
→ Lots of water (vitamins leach out when you drain it)

→ Use microwave-safe glass or ceramic, not regular plastic tubs
→ Cover food loosely and stir halfway for even heating
→ Make sure leftovers are piping hot all the way through

Steaming, quick stir-frying and microwaving all keep nutrients well.

Gluten-free is

Gluten-free has become a health trend. For most people, it's not a health upgrade.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley and rye.

Who truly needs to avoid it:
→ People with coeliac disease (diagnosed by a blood test and biopsy)
→ People with a wheat allergy
→ Some people with non-coeliac gluten sensitivity

→ They can be lower in fibre and higher in sugar or fat
→ They usually cost more

Naturally gluten-free foods like rice, millets, dal, fruit and vegetables are great — because they're whole foods, not because they're gluten-free.

Losing 100 hairs

Seeing hair on your pillow or in the shower drain? Some of it is completely normal.

→ Bald patches
→ A widening parting or thinning crown
→ Hair loss with fatigue, weight change or irregular periods

Trans fat is the worst fat for your heart. India has limited it — but it still turns up.

→ Vanaspati and some bakery shortenings
→ Street food fried in oil reused again and again
→ Some biscuits, puffs, khari and cream rolls

→ Choose freshly made food over deep-fried street snacks
→ Never reuse frying oil repeatedly at home

caption:
Cancer can feel random and out of our control. A large share of it isn't.

→ Excess body weight
→ Physical inactivity
→ Diets low in fruit, vegetables and fibre

→ HPV vaccine (prevents cervical cancer)
→ Hepatitis B vaccine (prevents liver cancer)
→ Screening for cervical, breast and oral cancer — catches it early

label: Reality check
headline:
Up 1 kg overnight
= fat gain?
body: Daily weight swings of 1–2 kg are mostly water, salt and food in your gut. Fat changes slowly. Watch the weekly average, not one day.
caption:
Stepped on the scale, saw +1 kg, and panicked? Relax. That's not fat.

To gain 1 kg of fat, you'd need to eat thousands of extra calories in a day.

What actually moves the scale day to day:
→ Water — especially after salty or carb-heavy meals
→ Food and waste still in your gut
→ Hormones and the menstrual cycle
→ A hard workout (muscles hold water while they repair)

How to track sensibly:
→ Weigh in the morning, after the toilet, before eating
→ Same scale, same conditions
→ Look at the weekly average, not single days
→ Track your waist too

Trends tell the truth. Single days tell stories.

label: Did you know

Red blood cells
live ~120 days.
body: Your body replaces millions of red blood cells every second. They need iron, B12 and folate to be made — which is why deficiencies cause anaemia.
caption:
Your blood is constantly being renewed. Right now, your bone marrow is making millions of red blood cells every second.

Each red blood cell lives about 120 days, carrying oxygen around your body, before it's recycled.

To make healthy red blood cells, your body needs:
→ Iron — dal, chana, green leafy veg, meat, eggs
→ Vitamin B12 — milk, curd, eggs, fish, meat
→ Folate — green leafy veg, legumes, citrus

Low on any of these → anaemia, tiredness and breathlessness.

Fun link: because red blood cells live about 3 months, the HbA1c test reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months.

Large studies have compared "weekend warriors" — people who get their weekly exercise in one or two days — with people who spread it across the week.

→ Warm up properly

→ Mix strength and cardio

body: When muscles are warm, hold gentle stretches for hamstrings, hips, chest and calves. Breathe slowly. Feel tension, never pain.
caption:
Stretching won't make you an athlete overnight, but it keeps your body moving freely as you age.

The best time for longer, held stretches is after your workout, when your muscles are warm.

A simple 5-minute routine:
→ Hamstrings: sit, reach towards your toes
→ Hip flexors: lunge position, push hips forward gently
→ Chest: hands on a door frame, lean through
→ Calves: hands on a wall, back heel down
→ Upper back: hug yourself and round your spine

Rules:
→ Hold each for 20–30 seconds
→ Breathe slowly
→ Feel a stretch, never sharp pain
→ No bouncing

Your brain uses
20% of energy.

Your brain is the hungriest organ you have.

It makes up about 2% of your body weight, but uses around 20% of your energy at rest.

That's why what you do affects how you think:
→ Poor sleep → foggy thinking and poor memory
→ Skipped meals → irritability and low focus
→ Dehydration → headaches and slower thinking
→ Exercise → better blood flow and new brain connections

Feed your brain well:
→ 7–9 hours of sleep
→ Regular meals with protein and fibre
→ Enough water
→ Daily movement
→ Learning something new

label: Water per ORS sachet
body:
Mix one WHO-ORS sachet in 1 litre
of clean water. Sip often during
diarrhoea or vomiting. Use within
24 hours. Too little water is risky.
caption:
ORS is one of the cheapest life-saving treatments in the world. But it has to be made correctly.

Diarrhoea and vomiting drain water and salts from your body fast — especially in children and older adults.

How to make ORS:
→ Wash your hands
→ Pour one full sachet into 1 litre of clean drinking water
→ Stir until fully dissolved
→ Sip small amounts often
→ Throw away what's left after 24 hours

Don't make it stronger with less water — it can make things worse.

Packaged "electrolyte" or sports drinks are not ORS. Look for "WHO formula" on the pack.

See a doctor for blood in stool, high fever, no urine for 6+ hours, or a very drowsy child.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Shaving makes hair
grow thicker?
body: Shaving cuts hair at the surface. It doesn't change the root, so hair doesn't grow back thicker, darker or faster. It just feels blunt.
caption:
"Don't shave, it'll grow back thicker." Generations have believed this one.

It isn't true.

Shaving cuts the hair at the skin's surface. It doesn't touch the follicle under the skin, which decides how thick, dark and fast your hair grows.

Why it seems thicker:
→ A shaved hair has a blunt tip, so it feels coarse
→ New hair hasn't been lightened by the sun yet
→ Short stubble stands straighter and is more visible

Shaving tips:
→ Use a sharp, clean razor
→ Shave after a bath, when hair is soft
→ Go with the direction of hair growth to reduce bumps

Shave, wax or leave it — it's your choice, not a health issue.

If you might become pregnant in the next year, this one is for you.

Folic acid (vitamin B9) helps prevent serious birth defects of the baby's brain and spine, called neural tube defects.

These develop in the first few weeks of pregnancy — often before you know you're pregnant.

→ Start at least 1 month before trying to conceive
→ Continue through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy

label: Reality check

Stretching stops

body: Research shows stretching before or after exercise barely reduces next-day soreness. Gradual progress, sleep and gentle movement help more.
caption:
Stretching after a workout to avoid sore legs tomorrow? It probably won't make much difference.

Muscle soreness that starts 24–72 hours after exercise (called DOMS) is normal, especially after new or harder workouts.

Reviews of many studies found that stretching before or after exercise has very little effect on this soreness.

What helps more:
→ Increase intensity gradually
→ Gentle movement the next day — walking, cycling
→ Good sleep
→ Enough protein and water
→ Time — it usually fades in 2–5 days

Stretching still helps flexibility and feels good. Just don't expect it to prevent soreness.

Sharp or joint pain isn't DOMS. Get it checked.

→ Strength often returns within weeks
→ Muscle regrows faster than it took to build originally

→ Build back up over a few weeks
→ Expect some soreness at first
